questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13941829/assets/1a54cae748796775b76ade4d9060d4eafe6bb84fd45ce725bd516a7db2681ba9.png)

The graph above shows the curve $y={(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}+c.$ Determine the value of $c$ and find the equation of the curve.
questions.worked_solution:
The horizontal asymptote of $y={(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}$ is $y=0.$ 

The vertical translation $y={(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}+c$ shifts the asymptote to $y=c.$

In the graph above, the horizontal asymptote is $y=2.$ Therefore, $c=2.$

questions.problem: Which of the following is the graph of  $y=3{(\frac{1}{6})}^{x}-1?$
questions.worked_solution:
We start with plotting the graph of $y={(\frac{1}{6})}^{x}:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13941829/assets/4cdc9e4fa78513bca01fa10242ba6c3f12b31c262448a8edf350c76e84b188b8.png)

Next, we plot the graph of $y=3{(\frac{1}{6})}^{x}.$ To do this, we scale the graph above by a factor of $3.$ The $y$-intercept moves from $(0,1)$ to $(0,3)$ but the horizontal asymptote stays at $y=0.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13941829/assets/8e7d6c5eb931f55a9f94ac33382c0e1ec9e9e49f50b3ab538d9848d6a77be665.png)

Finally, we plot the graph of $y=3{(\frac{1}{6})}^{x}-1.$ To do this, we shift the above graph $1$ unit down. The $y$-intercept moves from $(0,3)$ to $(0,2)$ and the horizontal asymptote moves from $y=0$ to $y=-1.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13941829/assets/9d332fa8d3d8ef65daaf34bf906c5ca7cd7e2edaf562386ed4e0ebc4555b0a64.png)

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the Shift and Stretch Applied to an Exponential Decay Curve
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13941829/assets/cdce64bf5d02850bbedc2b89af3b2e7447b733831c09d1955e4a9ee97e82d556.png)

The graph above shows $y=k{(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}+c.$ Find the value of $k-c.$
questions.worked_solution:
The horizontal asymptote of the curve $y=k{(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}+c$ is $y=c.$ In the graph above, the horizontal asymptote is $y=2.$ Hence, $c=2.$

We can solve for $k$ by finding a point on the graph and substituting for $x$ and $y.$ The labeled point on the graph is $(0,4),$ so we substitute $x=0$ and $y=4$ into the function and solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}k{(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}+c & =y \\ k{(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}+2 & =y \\ k{(\frac{1}{2})}^{0}+2 & =4 \\ k+2 & =4 \\ k & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
k-c=2-2=0.
$$

The equation of the curve is $y=2{(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}+2.$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13941829/assets/bc0e258229c74a97d61919440090dd7b2f0f4a200af987477d2be8818910a88b.png)

The graph above shows $y=k{(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}+c.$ Find the value of $k-c.$
questions.worked_solution:
The horizontal asymptote of the curve $y=k{(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}+c$ is $y=c.$ In the graph above, the horizontal asymptote is $y=\frac{1}{4},$ hence $c=\frac{1}{4}.$

We can solve for $k$ by finding a point on the graph and substituting for $x$ and $y.$ The labeled point on the graph is $(0,\frac{3}{2}),$ so we substitute $x=0$ and $y=\frac{3}{2}$ into the function and solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}k{(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}+c & =y \\ k{(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}+\frac{1}{4} & =y \\ k{(\frac{1}{2})}^{0}+\frac{1}{4} & =\frac{3}{2} \\ k+\frac{1}{4} & =\frac{3}{2} \\ k & =\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
k-c=\frac{5}{4}-\frac{1}{4}=1.
$$

The equation of the curve is $y=\frac{5}{4}{(\frac{1}{2})}^{x}+\frac{1}{4}.$
